stories.title: Huge security operation under way ahead of Trump visit
stories.summary: Gardaí have said the visit of US President Donald Trump to Ireland this weekend is one of the biggest security operations they have ever put in place. The force has declared an extraordinary event and it will see gardaí perform 10,000 12-hour shifts between today and Sunday. There will be disruption and traffic restrictions in Dublin and Clare during Mr Trump's visit. The first part of the visit tomorrow morning will be concentrated around Dublin Airport and the Phoenix Park and will result in road closures around these areas. He is expected to touch down on Air Force One at Dublin Airport tomorrow morning. There will be rolling road closures in place around the airport from 7.30am until 9.30am and between 11.30am and 1.30pm.

stories.title: Cullinane calls for 'accountability' over NAS allegations
stories.summary: Sinn Féin health spokesperson David Cullinane has called for accountability after more than 30 women alleged they experienced sexual harassment, misogyny, bullying or intimidation while working in the National Ambulance Service (NAS). The report, carried out by the HSE's Workplace Health and Wellbeing Unit, has not previously been published or reported on. Documents obtained by Prime Time also show that concerns about misogyny, gender discrimination and sexual harassment were raised with the Director of the NAS Robert Morton by senior management. NAS is a part of the HSE in which more than 2,400 staff are employed nationwide. Mr Cullinane described the issue as "deeply troubling", adding that there are "very serious questions for those at the very top and senior management levels within the National Ambulance Service" to answer. "There has to be an honesty, first of all, about the scale of the problem, and then there has to be accountability," he said.

stories.title: Oil falls but on track for 8% weekly gain on supply fears
stories.summary: Oil prices fell today but remained on course for a weekly gain of more than 8% while US diesel prices hit a record high as attacks along Middle East shipping routes stoked concerns about prolonged supply disruptions. Brent crude futures were down $2.68, or 2.5%, to $105 a barrel this evening, while US West Texas Intermediate crude fell $2.48, or 2.4%, to $100 a barrel. Both benchmarks hit their highest levels since mid-May earlier in the session. Both reversed early gains after the Financial Times reported that foreign ministers in the Middle East are trying to work out a temporary deal with Iran to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent and WTI rose more than 6% after an escalation in shipping attacks in the region yesterday. "Some headlines of possible new talks in the Middle East are weighing moderately on oil prices today," said UBS energy analyst Giovanni Staunovo. "I keep seeing near-term risks to the upside for oil prices, but we should expect ongoing high price volatility too."

stories.title: Houthis seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast - official
stories.summary: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have seized control of the country's entire Red Sea coast, a military official from the internationally recognised government said, consolidating the group's control of the vital waterway. The official said that all territory under government control "on the western coast has fallen", after the Houthis seized the strategic Mayyun Island and the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands in the Bab al-Mandab strait as they seek to choke off Saudi oil exports. Earlier, an official said, "Boats carrying armed Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island after government forces withdrew from it yesterday", referring to an island also known as Perim that divides the strait into lanes. "The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandeb area and Mayyun Island, which is located in the middle of the strait," he added, speaking on condition of anonymity. Hundreds of people have died since the Houthis launched an offensive against Riyadh-backed Yemeni government forces around Bab al-Mandeb last week. The waterway has gained importance as a transit route since the start of the wider Middle East war, which saw Iran blockade the Strait of Hormuz.

stories.title: Saints beat Hoops to blow title race wide open
stories.summary: First-half goals from Jay McClelland and Aidan Keena delivered St Patrick's Athletic a telling victory over champions Shamrock Rovers in a pulsating Dublin derby at Richmond Park to blow the SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division title race wide open. Having knocked holders Rovers out of the Club Orange Men's FAI Cup last month, Stephen Kenny’s Saints duly avenged their three league defeats to them earlier this year. Pat’s can now go top of the table on goal difference should they beat Dundalk at Oriel Park on Monday night, although Rovers, 10 points clear at the summit five weeks ago, will have a game in hand. That, though, is against arch-rivals Bohemians, who are also now just three points behind after recovering from 2-0 down to beat Galway United 3-2 at Eamonn Deacy Park. Starting with intent, St Pat’s were in front from their first attack of the game after just four minutes. Anchor midfielder Jamie Lennon was the architect, working a long-range one-two with Ryan Sheridan, the 17-year-old making his full league debut, to arc a superb cross to the far post. McClelland arrived to find the net off the underside of the crossbar with a side-foot volley for a stunning first league goal of the season.

stories.title: Minister expects integration congresses to happen in 2027
stories.summary: Minister for Sport Patrick O'Donovan says he doesn't expect there to be a long delay to the integration of all three Gaelic games bodies in the wake of Mary McAleese's resignation from the integration committee earlier this week. McAleese stepped away as the chairperson of the committee on Tuesday, a move which O'Donovan said was "really disappointing." The Minister met separately McAleese, as well as representatives from the GAA, the LGFA and the Camogie Association on Wednesday to get a sense of where the process was at, and he said that he expects integration to happen sooner rather than later. "This is the largest change in Gaelic Games administration since the foundation of the GAA in Hayes Hotel in 1884. The one thing is all of the bodies are signed up to it. "I asked a very straight question of all three of them yesterday - 'are you signed up to integration, a fully integrated single Gaelic Games organisation?' Special Congresses of the three Gaelic games bodies, which were planned for October, will not take place as final details around integration remain to be worked out.

stories.summary: Writer, director and composer Bobby Aherne introduces the new seaon below... If, like me, you've spent your life an avid imbiber of all forms of media, then the 'Geography’ section of your brain probably contains an entire atlas of places — largely islands — that don’t actually exist. From Gilligan’s Island to Yoshi’s one, isles Kirrin, Craggy, Monkey, Amity, Trash and Jurassic, and the rocks that hosted Truman Burbank, Mamma Mia! and McGoohan (debatably), we could probably navigate some nonexistent isles better than plenty of real places we’ve actually been to. Listen to the first episode of the latest series of Nero's Class Since yarn-spinners first started making stuff up, islands have proven to be the ideal setting for tall tales and fantastical fiction. See, islands can be whatever you want them to be: a blank canvas for the imagination, a self-contained microcosm of somewhere else, the perfect excuse to take your hero off-grid, and — in the case of somewhere like Summerisle — the most beautiful, picturesque, suffocating prison imaginable. In fiction, islands are almost always seen as a destination for some peace and quiet — two things that they rarely ever provide. I first became savvy to the poetic license provided by islands at some point in the mid-90s. After a family holiday to Inis Oírr, I took to writing a series of stories set somewhere called "Jeegara" — a far-away world made up entirely of 0-150 population islands with names like Jeesh Isle (named after my second class teacher’s favourite PG curse word), Gickile (home to Manure City and Fertiliser Bay), and The Grunki Scatter (your guess is as good as mine). Unfortunately, this creative streak happened to coincide with the opening of the Blanchardstown Centre just around the corner from my house — a development that sparked in me a simultaneous interest in liminal spaces, foreign franchises and mall mapping. In a confusing twist, this meant that all of my meticulously sketched, far-fetched fantasy lands ended up having their very own branches of Tuthills, Roches Stores, Smyths Toys and La Croissanterie. Capitalism had seeped into both the suburbs and my 9-year-old brain, which was seemingly only too eager to also help hoosh it out to a bunch of archipelagos in imaginary distant galaxies.

stories.title: Céline Dion poised for emotional comeback in Paris
stories.summary: Céline Dion is set to make her long-awaited return to the stage in Paris tonight after years battling a rare neurological disorder, with fans counting down the hours until showtime. The My Heart Will Go On singer will perform her first full concert in six years, marking a major milestone in her comeback after Stiff Person Syndrome forced her to cancel shows and left her struggling to sing. Around 30,000 fans are expected at the Plenitude Arena outside Paris for the sold-out opening night of the 58-year-old Canadian's 26-date run in the French capital. Some made the pilgrimage a day early, heading to the venue on Friday evening to soak up the atmosphere ahead of the Québec-born hitmaker's return. "She's a legend, she's iconic," said Chloe Rydquist, who travelled from London with her wife, Katy. "For her to have this comeback, we were, like, 'We need to be there for the first night'," she added.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (September 11-13)
stories.summary: From sunset gigs to a Dolly Parton tribute night, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. Following an incredible summer of sold-out sunset gigs, SETS at Guinness Storehouse is preparing for the ultimate series finale. The fourth and final event will see Derry-born artist SOAK headline and curate a very special evening of Irish music on Friday, 11 September 2026. Gilla Band will take guests into the night as they get behind the decks for an exclusive DJ set. Ticket Price: €30 (Includes a complimentary Guinness or a non-alcoholic alternative). Strictly Over 21s. Hannah Mooney's latest exhibition is set to light up the Dublin art scene this September. Lightshift, an exploration of light and atmosphere in the west of Ireland, will take place in Gormleys, Dublin 2, from September 10 - 30. This marks her first solo exhibition in Ireland and brings together a significant body of work. Free to enter. Wing Fest returns to Brickyard, Dundrum, from 10–13 September. Following a hugely successful outing earlier this summer, the Brickyard kitchen team is bringing the festival back for a special birthday edition. Guests can expect the return of much-loved favourites, including duck wings and vegetarian cauliflower wings, alongside some of the most popular sauces and flavours, plus a couple of exciting new additions created especially for the occasion. From 5 - 20 September 2026, Dublin will be overrun with live theatre, dance, wrestling, stand-up comedy, and much more. Experience 16 days and nights of bold new performance across theatres, clubs, streets, parks, pubs and unexpected city spaces. For its 32nd edition, the jam-packed festival is working to reflect Ireland of today. Find the full programme of events here. Ireland's annual Mexican festival returns to the National Stadium in Dublin 8 on Saturday, 12 September, from 3pm. Expect seven live bands, five dance groups, two DJs, and a long line of food vendors and markets. Join the Mexican community and friends to celebrate the 216th Anniversary of Mexico's Independence and experience Mexican culture. Tickets €22.42.

stories.title: Trump meets President in Dublin ahead of Doonbeg visit
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump arrived at Áras an Uachtaráin in the Phoenix Park and shook hands with President Catherine Connolly shortly after 9am. President Connolly stood at the end of the steps in the Portico to greet Mr Trump and then led the US president down the Francini corridor and into the state reception room. President Connolly, a long-standing critic of the US president, invited him to sign the visitors' book in the state reception room. They then proceeded to the drawing room and into a hallway where Mr Trump was introduced to dignitaries. Air Force One touched down at Dublin Airport just before 8.30am, where President Trump was welcomed by Tánaiste Simon Harris, who earlier said the trip is an opportunity to mark and reflect on the "deep and enduring" links between Ireland and the United States. Speaking at Dublin Airport, Mr Harris said; "talking to the President there at the foot of Air Force One we had an opportunity to recall previous conversations we had, indeed I had phoned President Trump on his election as President of the United States.

stories.title: Harris signals cut in home heating oil tax
stories.summary: The Tánaiste has strongly suggested that the Government will cut tax on home heating oil in the Budget. The Government has two options when it comes to reducing the cost of home heating oil. It can lower the carbon tax on kerosene, something Sinn Féin is expected to introduce legislation on in the Dáil next week. Alternatively, it could equalise the VAT rate charged on home heating oil, which is currently 13.5%, with the 9% levied on gas. The latter approach has been proposed by the industry group, Fuels for Ireland. Mr Harris is also expected to commit to increasing the threshold at which workers pay the higher rate of income tax in each of the next four budgets.

stories.title: Fines for social media firms counterproductive - minister
stories.summary: Minister for Communications Patrick O'Donovan has said that fines imposed on social media firms are "free advertising" for platforms and have become counterproductive. He was speaking at the opening of an EU Presidency conference in Dublin Castle on online safety which is hearing from policymakers, industry figures, representative organisations, regulators and children. Mr O'Donovan said Europe is moving towards stricter controls on social media and moving away from just imposing fines. "Fines are really important; the money goes back into the Exchequer," Mr O'Donovan said. "But these companies are gleaning enormous amounts of free advertising out of these fines, and it is actually, in many ways, becoming counterproductive," he added. The Communications Minister said that if the media regulator Coimisiún na Meán requests additional powers to ban platforms that are harmful to children, he would be open to considering it.

stories.title: UK economy grows at fastest pace since February 2025
stories.summary: The UK economy grew at the fastest annual pace in 18 months in July, helped by a boost from artificial intelligence and extending a strong first-half performance despite headwinds from the US-Iran war, official figures showed today. British gross domestic product in July was 1.6% higher than a year earlier, the fastest annual rate since February 2025 and above economists' 1.2% forecast, the Office for National Statistics figures showed today. The economy grew 0.4% on the month in July, compared with median expectations in a Reuters poll for output to be unchanged, and output in the three months to July - which smooths volatility - was also stronger than expected at 0.4%. Much of the growth over the past three months appeared to come from businesses involved in computer programming that were benefiting from the AI boom, the ONS' Director of Economic Statistics, Liz McKeown, said. "Looking at the latest month, services also drove growth in July, with computer programming again making the largest contribution," she added, noting an extra boost for some firms from the men's soccer World Cup and unusually hot weather. Sterling was little changed against the US dollar after the data and economists had mixed views about whether Britain's current economic outperformance would be sustained in the run-up to finance minister John Healey's first budget next month.

stories.title: Coastal erosion forces cancellation of US music festival
stories.summary: A music festival set to feature The Killers, Olivia Dean and Jack White was cancelled because the California beach where it was to be held has been eaten away by coastal erosion. The two-day Ocean Way Festival had been planned for later this month in Santa Monica, but waves up to 4.5 meters and storm runoff have left the beach in the city near Los Angeles badly degraded, forcing local officials to pull the plug. "Storm surf generated by Hurricane Marie and runoff from a storm drain outfall eroded a large portion of the festival site," said a statement from the city of Santa Monica. The storm, which churned the waters of the Pacific over the last week, stripped sand off the beach, making it no longer safe to hold the festival there, the city said. "The surf took the beach we planned this on, and we cannot put tens of thousands of festival-goers on that sand until it's safe," said Mayor Caroline Torosis. The coastal city of Santa Monica - the official end point of Route 66 - has a wide stretch of golden sand and a large wooden pier that features frequently in American television shows and movies.

stories.title: Excited Hunt open to surprises in new streamlined pathway
stories.summary: If there's one thing Noel Hunt is not short of, it's enthusiasm. And life within the Republic of Ireland underage coaching set-up seems to have given him an even greater pep in his step. Back in May, the ex-Boys in Green striker was announced as one of the five new international lead coaches appointed as part of a revamp of the structures within the FAI. Along with three-time senior cap Hunt, the quintet of lead coaches is made up of Chelsea Noonan, John Cotter, Keith O'Halloran and James Scott. Rather than being assigned and restricted to a specific age grade as was the policy in the past, they will all move fluidly between the under-15 and under-19s in both the men's and women's pathways. They will be supported by full-time international coaches Conor McCormack, Graham Gartland, Mark Connors and Richie Smith. All will be required to familiarise themselves with a broader range of emerging talents than was customary in previous eras.

stories.summary: All-Ireland senior champions Galway lead the way with 14 nominations for the 2026 TG4 All-Star Awards. The Tribeswomen claimed a second Brendan Martin Cup success at Croke Park on 2 August. Runners-up Kerry have 12 players nominated in the 45-player long list. Ulster champions Armagh are next in line with six, Dublin and Lidl National League Division 1 winners Cork have three each, there are two apiece for Waterford, Kildare and Mayo, and a Meath nominee completes the list compiled by the Ladies Gaelic Football Association's All-Star committee. For Galway, Leah O'Halloran is nominated, along with defenders Kate Geraghty (captain and All-Ireland final player of the match), Sarah Ní Loingsigh, Brónagh Quinn, Hannah Noone and Nicola Ward. At midfield, sisters Niamh and Siobhán Divilly are both nominated, while another Divilly sister, Olivia, is one of six Galway forwards up for recognition alongside Kate Slevin, Kate Thompson, Leanne Coen, Róisín Leonard and Eva Noone, sister of Hannah.

stories.title: Celtic get 'general behaviour' warning for Rangers clash
stories.summary: Martin O'Neill revealed Celtic were given a "general behaviour" warning by Police Scotland ahead of Sunday’s Premier Sports Cup quarter-final against Rangers at Ibrox. There will be no Hoops fans in the 50,000-capacity stadium at the order of the authorities amid a ticket allocation spat between the two Glasgow giants. The spat is partly a result of the last Old Firm clash in Govan in March, which was marred by fans’ disorder as Celtic won the Scottish Gas Scottish Cup quarter-final on penalties after a goalless 120 minutes. The two clubs have both been ordered to play their next home Scottish Cup matches behind closed doors and have also been handed a £100,000 compensation bill, paid to whichever team is drawn as the away side in their next respective fixtures in that competition. The 74-year-old Hoops boss admitted that "it’ll be a bit strange not having the (Celtic) fans in but I’m nervously and excitedly looking forward to it, it’s a great fixture" and also spoke about the police visit. O’Neill said: "We had the police come in today, just a little 15 minute meeting with us, just reminders of our behaviour, which I think is actually a timely reminder. It a good thing as well.

stories.title: True Dub Flood excited for rugby's Tallaght debut
stories.summary: Having togged out in green at the Aviva Stadium, Ringsend native Stacey Flood has said she cannot wait for Ireland's Tallaght debut on Sunday, 20 September. By her own admission, Flood is a true Dub, steeped in a Dublin sporting family. Her sister Kim also represented Leinster and Ireland in rugby as well as the Dublin ladies Gaelic footballers. That passion is present in the stands, meaning the Ireland full-back is expecting the full clan to turn out when Ireland play host to the USA. Speaking at the launch of the IRFU's new men's and women's jerseys last week, the 30-year-old could not withhold her excitement for the latest road trip of this team's tour around the country. "It feels like I'm playing at home every time I play in Dublin and throughout my career, I didn't get to do that often, playing sevens; so, every time we play in Dublin, I know half the Flood family is going to be there, even when we play everywhere else actually, they're always there. "I feel like everyone has their communities, like Béibhinn (Parsons) and Aoibheann (Reilly) being from Galway, they get so (much) support there and I feel like I'm not a country girl, I'm like everyone in Dublin supports me. "They might not know me but that's how I make it in my head, I'm like everyone's there to support me because I'm a Dub. I feel like it's different in the country, but I just try to replicate that for Dublin for myself."

stories.title: Nicole Flattery awarded 2026 Rooney Prize for Irish Literature
stories.summary: Nicole Flattery has been named the recipient of the 2026 Rooney Prize for Irish Literature at a gala dinner in Trinity College Dublin. The award, which marks its 50th anniversary this year, recognises an outstanding body of work by an emerging Irish writer under the age of 40. The annual prize has been doubled this year from €10,000 to €20,000 to mark the anniversary. The change was announced by the benefactor and custodian of the prize, Dr Peter Rooney. The oldest-established literary award in Ireland, The Rooney Prize is administered by the Oscar Wilde Centre for Creative Writing at Trinity College Dublin. Ms Flattery, originally from Kinnegad, Co Westmeath, was presented with the award at the event, which was attended by guests from the world of Irish literature, including 21 previous Rooney Prize winners. Previous recipients include Kate Cruise O'Brien (1979), Neil Jordan (1981), Frank McGuinness (1985), Glenn Patterson (1988), Anne Enright (1991), Colum McCann (1994), Mike McCormack (1996), Claire Keegan (2000), Claire Kilroy (2004), Kevin Barry (2007), Lucy Caldwell (2011), Doireann Ní Ghríofa (2016), Mark O’Connell (2019), Seán Hewitt (2022), Michael Magee (2023), and Suad Aldarra (2024).

stories.title: Gaza film, Martin McDonagh's latest vie for Venice honour
stories.summary: The Venice Film Festival hands out its top awards tonight after two weeks of often dark, violent programming, including a chilling Israeli-made documentary about Gaza and an oddball drama from writer-director Martin McDonagh starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell. NAZA, which features Israeli whistleblowers analysing the mass killing of civilians in Gaza, earned a record 25-minute standing ovation at its premiere on Thursday and is the highest-scored film by international critics, according to the film magazine Screen. But it faces competition from other well-received films, including the poignant relationship study Possible Love by South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong, and the dark comedy Wild Horse Nine by London Irish director Martin McDonagh. Watch: Martin McDonagh discusses Wild Horse Nine at the Venice Film Festival The latter features Malkovich playing a jaded CIA agent taking a break with a colleague (Sam Rockwell) on Easter Island in Chile ahead of the 1973 American-backed military coup there in a performance that has seen him tipped by some critics for Oscar glory. As the director of one of the few films that had audiences laughing in Venice, director McDonagh said his acid sense of humour was his way of coping with the state of the world.

stories.title: Batten down the political hatches, Trump is in town
stories.summary: The diplomatic and security arms of the State have been preparing for weeks, if not months, for the arrival of US President Donald Trump to counties Dublin and Clare later today. But the problem when it comes to President Trump is that even the most meticulous of planning can sometimes come undone in a split second. From a security perspective, the Dublin leg of what gardaí are calling one of the biggest security operations in the history of the State will be much easier to handle. Mr Trump's engagements in the capital are confined to the closed-off space of the Phoenix Park. In this way, his Dublin trip will resemble his second state visit to Britain last year - where he largely stayed within the confines of Windsor Castle and was shielded away from the tens of thousands of protesters in central London. "I’m confident that thousands of people will be on the streets tomorrow to oppose the world’s biggest warmonger," said People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy ahead of a planned demonstration in Dublin this afternoon.

stories.title: TikTok has 'change of heart' and will attend committee
stories.summary: TikTok will attend the Oireachtas Committee on Media later this month, having initially rejected an invite, Labour TD and commitee chair Alan Kelly has said. Last month, TikTok declined an invitation to discuss the posting of illegal criminal videos on social media platforms. At the time, the social-media firm said it felt it could not attend the committtee due to the ongoing garda investigation into last month's M9 motorway crash and a Coimisiún na Meán examination of social media content relating to the incident. It also said it did not feel it would be appropriate for it to be the only platform to attend the media committee meeting on the issue However, in a statement today, Mr Kelly said TikTok had a "change of heart" and had now decided to attend the committee hearing on Wednesday 23 September. "I very much welcome the decision of TikTok to now attend our Oireachtas Committee meeting on September 23.

stories.title: PBP propose data centre levy to fund €500 energy credit
stories.summary: People Before Profit-Solidarity has proposed that data centres should be forced to pay the same percentage of tax on their electricity as ordinary households. Outlining the proposal at the party's think-in in Dublin this afternoon, it said the €1.5 billion raised from the move would be used to fund a €500 energy credit for homes and additional funding for disability services. Under the plans, which will be tabled in a private members motion in the Dáil next week, the party wants to double the amount of tax data centres pay on their electricity to be doubled from 20c per KWh to 40c per KWh - the same amount as an ordinary household. Outlining the proposal to reporters, PBP-Solidarity TD Paul Murphy said the move would raise €1.5bn extra for the exchequer every year, and would be used to fund a €500 energy credit and for homes as well as extra funding and supports for children with disabilities. "Data centres pay half the price for the electricity they use. We would use that money [the €1.5bn fund] to shield people from the cost-of-living crisis." Party members also said they want to see a wealth tax introduced in the upcoming budget which would target individuals with a net worth of €5m or more, which the party said would raise €9bn for the exchequer which could be re-routed to fund other areas.

stories.title: US consumer inflation picks up in August
stories.summary: US consumer prices accelerated ⁠in August as the cost of gasoline rebounded after two monthly declines in a row, bolstering financial market expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates next week. The US Consumer Price Index increased 0.4% last month after edging up 0.1% in July, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said today. In the 12 months to August, consumer inflation advanced 3.4% after rising by the same margin in July. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI increasing 0.4% over the month and climbing 3.4% year-on-year. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI rose 0.3% last month after gaining 0.2% in July. The so-called core CPI increased 2.4% year-on-year in August after rising 2.5% in July. The US Fed tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures price indexes for its 2% inflation target. The US government reported earlier this week ‌an increase in the Producer Price Index in ⁠August, with strong rises in several key components that feed into the calculation of PCE inflation. That added to last week's robust employment report for August in boosting rate hike prospects next week.

stories.title: Zelensky urges US to sanction Russia 'now' over strikes
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump's administration should immediately impose new sanctions on Russia over recent deadly strikes on Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said. The comments came after Mr Zelensky announced he planned to meet Mr Trump in late September, amid US-led efforts to broker an end to the four-and-a-half year Ukraine war. "Sanctions need to be imposed now," Mr Zelensky told the Yalta European Strategy forum. "Honestly, I sometimes do not understand why decisions cannot be made quickly," he added. Mr Zelensky separately called for a truce with Russia covering strikes on energy targets, saying Ukraine was ready to hit back if Russia attacked his country's energy grid over the winter. "Russia knows that if they strike, they will receive the same in return," he said.

stories.title: McCartan's club focus after Westmeath family fortunes
stories.summary: In the space of a little under 24 hours earlier this summer, Westmeath's Lara McCartan and three of her siblings found themselves enjoying memorable provincial championship successes. Having been part of the team that won the same title the year before, Lara and Lucy McCartan were back in harness to help the Lake County overcome Wexford on a scoreline of 4-20 to 4-08 in the Leinster intermediate final at Cedral St Conleth’s Park in Newbridge on 16 May. A day later, their brother Sam started at centre half-forward and scored two points when the Westmeath men’s footballers defeated Dublin to secure their first Leinster senior football championship crown in 22 years at Croke Park. A fourth member of the McCartan family – Danny - was also a member of the match-day panel as the midlanders held their nerve to record an extra-time victory in GAA HQ. Interestingly, Dublin’s top scorer from play in this game was their recently retired stalwart Ciarán Kilkenny, who is a cousin of the McCartan’s on their mother’s side. "You couldn’t have written it," McCartan recalled of that eventful weekend in May.
